blocks.text: How the first-time buyer PTT exemption works

parts.t: BC calls its land transfer tax the property transfer tax (PTT). It's charged on the fair market value of the home, in brackets that rise with the price. If you qualify as a first-time buyer, the first $500,000 is exempt. On a home above $500,000 you pay the regular rates on the rest, up to the price limits in the programs table above.
The 5% rate applies to the residential portion over $3,000,000.
The first $500,000 is exempt, so you only pay PTT on the last $10,000. The full PTT bill is $8,200, the exemption covers $8,000, and $200 is owing.

blocks.text: Example: $500,000 home in Langley with a partner who isn't a first-time buyer

parts.t: When you buy with someone who doesn't qualify, the exemption only applies to your share. If you each own 50%, you get 50% of the $8,000 exemption, which is $4,000. The other $4,000 is owing.

blocks.text: Who counts as a first-time buyer

parts.t: BC's test is stricter than the federal one. For the PTT exemption, you can never have owned an interest in a principal residence anywhere in the world. The federal Home Buyers' Plan only looks back four years, so someone who sold a home more than four years ago can count as a first-time buyer federally but not for BC's PTT exemption. Who qualifies as a first-time home buyer in British Columbia?

To qualify for BC’s First-Time Home Buyers’ Property Transfer Tax Exemption, you must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, have lived in BC for 12 consecutive months immediately before registration (or filed at least 2 BC income tax returns in the past 6 years), and have never owned a registered interest in a principal residence anywhere in the world at any time.
What is the BC First-Time Home Buyers’ Property Transfer Tax exemption limit in 2026?

Since April 1, 2024, qualifying first-time buyers pay zero BC Property Transfer Tax on the first $500,000 of a principal residence’s fair market value when the purchase price is $835,000 or less (saving up to $8,000). A partial phased-out exemption applies between $835,000 and $860,000, and properties over $860,000 or larger than 0.5 hectares do not receive the full exemption.
How does the BC Newly Built Home Exemption work for first-time and move-up buyers?

If you buy a newly built condo, townhome, or house in BC with a fair market value of $1,100,000 or less and move in as your principal residence, you can qualify for a full BC Property Transfer Tax exemption of up to $20,000, with a partial exemption phasing out between $1,100,000 and $1,150,000.
Can I combine the First Home Savings Account (FHSA) and the RRSP Home Buyers’ Plan (HBP)?

Yes. Qualifying first-time buyers in Canada can combine tax-free FHSA withdrawals (up to $8,000 per year in contribution room, $40,000 lifetime limit per person) with RRSP Home Buyers’ Plan withdrawals (up to $60,000 per person, repaid over 15 years starting the second year after the withdrawal, or the fifth year for first withdrawals made from 2022 to 2025, with a proposed extension of that relief to December 31, 2028) on the same home purchase.
What happens if I buy a home in BC with a partner who is not a first-time buyer?

BC calculates the First-Time Home Buyers’ Property Transfer Tax Exemption based on each buyer’s proportional registered interest on title. If you qualify as a first-time buyer and take a 50% share on title with a partner who has owned a home before, you can still claim 50% of the eligible exemption.
How long must I live in the home to keep my BC First-Time Home Buyers’ PTT exemption?

For an existing home, you must move into the property within 92 days of the date it is registered at the Land Title Office and continue to occupy it as your principal residence for the remainder of the first year after registration to retain the full exemption.
